title: Human Skin Anatomy: Epidermis, Dermis & Cutaneous Guide
description: Discover human skin anatomy across the stratified epidermis, collagen-rich dermis, subcutaneous hypodermis, hair follicles, sweat glands, and nerve fibers.
h1: Human Skin Anatomy: Epidermis, Dermis, Glands and Sensory Nerves
blurb: Our largest organ combines a self-renewing stratified epidermis with a collagen-rich dermis housing sweat glands, hair follicles, blood vessels, and touch nerves.
lead: Covering roughly two square meters in an average adult, the skin is our largest organ—acting simultaneously as a waterproof shield, radiator, and sensory surface. In this illustrated guide to human skin anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including stratum corneum, stratum basale & spinosum, dermis (papillary & reticular), hypodermis (subcutis)—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Covering roughly two square meters in an average adult, the skin is our largest organ—acting simultaneously as a waterproof shield, radiator, and sensory surface. The epidermis is a keratinising stratified squamous epithelium renewed from the basal layer every ~4 weeks, with melanocytes, Langerhans cells and Merkel cells among the keratinocytes. Beneath it the dermis gives strength and elasticity (papillary loose, reticular dense connective tissue) and carries the vessels, nerves, hair follicles and glands. The hypodermis is fat that insulates and cushions. Skin makes vitamin D, senses the world, and regulates temperature by sweating and by shunting blood through arteriovenous anastomoses. Within the human body, the skin (Cutis) is situated in whole body surface — the largest organ, receives arterial perfusion via dermal plexuses from segmental perforators, and is innervated by somatic sensory (touch, pain, temperature) + sympathetic.

Structurally, the stratum corneum comprises 15–20 layers of dead, flattened, keratin-filled corneocytes held by lipids — the "brick and mortar" barrier. Physiologically, the stratum corneum governs waterproofing and the main barrier to microbes and chemicals. The stratum basale & spinosum (Stratum basale) is the single basal row of dividing keratinocytes on the basement membrane, plus the prickle-cell layers above with desmosomes, melanocytes and Langerhans cells. Physiologically, the stratum basale & spinosum governs renews the epidermis; melanocytes transfer pigment; Langerhans cells present antigen. Structurally, the dermis (papillary & reticular) (Dermis) comprises papillary layer of loose connective tissue forming dermal papillae; reticular layer of dense irregular collagen and elastin. Physiologically, the dermis (papillary & reticular) governs strength, elasticity, sensation and the vascular supply of the epidermis. Structurally, the hypodermis (subcutis) (Tela subcutanea) comprises loose connective tissue and fat, with larger vessels and nerves and, in places, panniculus carnosus. Physiologically, the hypodermis (subcutis) governs insulation, energy store, shock absorption and skin mobility. The hair shaft & follicle (Folliculus pili) is a keratinised shaft growing from a follicle that dips into dermis or fat, with a bulb around a dermal papilla and a bulge of stem cells. Physiologically, the hair shaft & follicle governs protection, sensation and (in other mammals) insulation. The arrector pili muscle (Musculus arrector pili) is a band of smooth muscle from follicle to dermis, supplied by sympathetic fibres. Physiologically, the arrector pili muscle governs erects the hair (goose flesh) and helps express sebum.

Clinically, regarding the stratum corneum, its thickness defines palms and soles; loss in burns allows catastrophic fluid and heat loss. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the stratum basale & spinosum, basal cell carcinoma arises here at sun-exposed sites; melanoma from melanocytes. Clinically, the dermis (papillary & reticular) split-thickness grafts take from the dermal remnants left in the wound bed; keloids are dermal over-scarring. Medical evaluation of the hypodermis (subcutis) also notes that subcutaneous insulin absorption varies with site and temperature because of this layer's blood flow.

questions.question: What are the main layers of the skin?
questions.answer: The epidermis is the outer epithelial barrier; the vascular dermis contains connective tissue, vessels and nerves. Subcutaneous tissue lies beneath the skin and varies by region. Structurally, the hypodermis (subcutis) (Tela subcutanea) comprises loose connective tissue and fat, with larger vessels and nerves and, in places, panniculus carnosus. Physiologically, the hypodermis (subcutis) governs insulation, energy store, shock absorption and skin mobility.

questions.question: How does skin help protect the body?
questions.answer: The keratinized epidermal surface limits water loss and helps block external injury and microbes, while deeper tissue supports sensation, repair and temperature regulation. Structurally, the stratum granulosum comprises flattened keratinocytes with keratohyalin granules and lipid-releasing lamellar bodies. Physiologically, the stratum granulosum governs builds the water-permeability barrier.
